claims.text: Mastercard announced Agent Pay on 2025-04-29 as its Agentic Payments Program.
The launch release says Agent Pay introduces Mastercard Agentic Tokens that build on Mastercard's existing tokenization capabilities.
The tokenization capabilities named in the launch release include mobile contactless payments, secure card-on-file and Mastercard Payment Passkeys.
Agent Pay is a proprietary Mastercard program with no public specification, version number or governance body of its own.
Mastercard's developer guides refer readers to the Mastercard Agent Pay Acceptance Framework for full details, and that framework specification is not public.
Agent Pay is not AP2: AP2 is Google's open protocol, while Agent Pay is a card-network program run by Mastercard.

Mastercard's launch, regional and developer-guide pages describe agentic tokens as built on Mastercard tokenization and do not name MDES; developer pages mention MDES only for Virtual Card Tokens and Token Connect enrollment.
Mastercard's Agentic Tokens and Visa's agentic network tokens are separate products issued by separate networks.
Verifiable Intent is published under the Apache-2.0 license in the GitHub repository agent-intent/verifiable-intent.
The Verifiable Intent README says the project is maintained by Mastercard and open to multi-stakeholder contribution.
The Verifiable Intent specification lists its authors as the Verifiable Intent Working Group.
The agent-intent/verifiable-intent repository was created on GitHub on 2026-03-05.
FIDO Alliance describes Verifiable Intent as co-developed with Google and designed to work with AP2.
Mastercard contributed Verifiable Intent to the FIDO Alliance on 2026-04-28, the same day Google contributed AP2.
FIDO says the AP2 and Verifiable Intent contributions are to be developed in its Payments Technical Working Group, chaired by members from Mastercard and Visa.
FIDO's Payments Working Group was launched on 2025-04-29, so only the Agentic Authentication Technical Working Group was new on 2026-04-28.
The 2025-04-29 launch release names Microsoft as a collaborator on agentic commerce use cases with Azure OpenAI Service and Copilot Studio.
The launch release names IBM and its watsonx Orchestrate product for business-to-business use cases.
The launch release names Braintree and Checkout.com as acquirers and checkout players that will extend their tokenization for agentic payments.
The launch release says the program will require trusted AI agents to be registered and verified before they can pay on behalf of users.
The launch release says every party in the value chain will be able to recognize transactions facilitated by agents.
The launch release promises a process to help clarify agentic transactions that may be unfamiliar or unrecognized.
On 2025-09-10 Mastercard said all US Mastercard cardholders would be enabled for Agent Pay by the holiday season, with a global rollout to follow.
The 2025-09-10 release says Citi and U.S. Bank Mastercard cardholders would be the first to experience AI-enabled shopping.
The 2025-09-10 release names Stripe, Google and Ant International's Antom as AI and commerce collaborators and PayOS as a provider going live.
The 2025-09-10 release announced the Agent Toolkit, Agent Sign-Up, Insight Tokens and Agentic Consulting Services.
The 2025-09-10 release says Mastercard was working with the FIDO Alliance Payments Working Group on a verifiable credential standard confirming amount, merchant and product.
PayOS announced on 2025-10-01 that it executed the first live agentic payment using a Mastercard Agentic Token.
Mastercard Developers says initial Agent Pay documentation pages went live on 2025-10-16 for early preview.
Mastercard's December 2025 release says the Agent Pay Acceptance Framework launched in October 2025; no source read gives the exact day.
Cloudflare published its post on securing agentic commerce with Visa and Mastercard on 2025-10-24.
On 2025-10-27 Mastercard and PayPal said Agent Pay would be integrated into PayPal's wallet.
PayPal said it would pilot the Mastercard Agent Pay Acceptance Framework.
On the 2025-10-30 earnings call Mastercard's CEO said the first agentic transaction took place on its network that quarter.
On the 2025-10-30 earnings call Mastercard said U.S. Bank and Citi cardholders could use Agent Pay and the remaining US issuers would be enabled in November 2025.
On the 2025-10-30 earnings call Mastercard described its acceptance framework as letting merchants participate without significant development or integration.
On 2025-12-03 Mastercard announced that Agent Pay would launch across Latin America and the Caribbean beginning in 2026.
Mastercard said issuers in Latin America would be enabled for Agent Pay by February 2026.
Mastercard named Bemobi, Checkout.com, Davivienda, Evertec, Getnet, Inti, MagaluPay and Yuno as early Latin American enabling partners.
Mastercard completed Australia's first authenticated agentic transactions, announced on 2026-01-28, with a CBA debit card and a Westpac credit card.
The Australian transactions bought Event Cinemas tickets and Thredbo accommodation, were processed through IPSI and used Maincode's Matilda model.
Commonwealth Bank of Australia described its participation as early, controlled trials with Mastercard.
On 2026-03-02 Santander and Mastercard said they completed Europe's first live end-to-end payment executed by an AI agent.
Santander ran the transaction in a controlled environment on its live payments infrastructure, and the release says it is not a commercial rollout.
PayOS supported the end-to-end orchestration of the Santander transaction.
On 2026-03-03 Stripe extended Shared Payment Tokens to carry Mastercard Agent Pay and Visa Intelligent Commerce agentic network tokens.
Stripe says agentic network tokens map to the latest funding PAN at authorization and add information to the authorization message for issuers.
Mastercard announced Verifiable Intent on 2026-03-05.
PYMNTS reported commitments to Verifiable Intent from Google, Fiserv, IBM, Checkout.com, Basis Theory and Getnet.
Mastercard's developer guides name Google, IBM, Fiserv, Checkout.com, Worldpay and Adyen as Verifiable Intent partners.
Mastercard said integration of Verifiable Intent into Agent Pay's intent APIs was expected in the coming months.
Mastercard announced Korea's first live authenticated agentic transaction on 2026-03-17, a ride booked through hoppa by a CardInfoLink agent.
The Korea release lists Agent Pay launches in the US in 2025 and in Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Malaysia and India in 2026.
On 2026-03-24 Mastercard said 17 issuers and processors completed live agentic transactions across Latin America and the Caribbean.
Mastercard says the 2026-03-24 Latin American transactions were performed in controlled environments.
The 2026-03-24 release says Mastercard is embedding Verifiable Intent directly into the payment flow.
Mastercard says nearly 100% of issuers in Latin America are enabled with its tokenization technology.
On 2026-06-02 Mastercard said all Mastercard issuers in Europe are enabled at a network level for Agent Pay.
Mastercard listed 36 European banks that completed controlled live agentic transactions on Priceless.com with payOS orchestration.
Mastercard, Worldline and ING performed a live end-to-end agentic transaction with all elements of the flow based in Europe.
Mastercard launched Agent Pay for Machines (AP4M) on 2026-06-10 for high-frequency, low-latency, low-value payments by agents and machines.
Mastercard says AP4M supports credentialing, permissioning, transacting and settling across cards, accounts and stablecoins.
The AP4M release says every agent is credentialed and can be recognized with Verifiable Intent.
The AP4M release names 32 initial participants and supporters, one of which is Mastercard Merchant Cloud.
AP4M participants include Coinbase, Stripe, Tempo, Polygon, Solana Foundation, Cloudflare, Adyen, Checkout.com and Skyfire.
The AP4M release publishes no pricing, API or settlement schedule.
On 2026-09-30 Mastercard named the Agent Pay Trust Framework, which brings together identity, intent, controls, execution and intelligence.
On 2026-09-30 Mastercard began US testing of a probability score indicating the likelihood that a transaction was initiated by an AI agent.
Mastercard named Skyfire, a Know Your Agent provider, as a partner for recognizing trusted agents on 2026-09-30.
The 2026-09-30 release says Mastercard and Cloudflare are exploring how web and payment network signals can give visibility into AI-powered transactions in privacy-preserving environments.
No white paper for the Agent Pay Trust Framework was found; the 2026-09-30 release links none.
Mastercard's developer guide says only registered agents can transact through the network.
Mastercard says each agent goes through a security review before certification and certified agents are added to trusted agent lists maintained by the networks.
Mastercard says merchants register for Agent Pay through their acquirer or payment service provider.
Mastercard's certification criteria require agents to authenticate consumers, use tokenized credentials, capture consumer intent accurately and follow privacy rules.
Mastercard says agentic tokens may be single-use, merchant-specific or time-limited depending on the authorization.
Mastercard says agents cannot use a consumer's existing card on file at a merchant because the network could not then recognize the transaction as agentic.
At Levels 1 and 2 the agent types the token into the merchant's standard card form, and the token looks like a card number to the merchant.
Mastercard says merchants accepting agent tokens keep their PCI scope unchanged.
Mastercard documents the Signature-Input parameters keyid, alg, created, expires, nonce and tag for agent request signatures.
Mastercard's Level 1 guide says Mastercard Agent Pay agents use the tag value Agent-pay-auth.
Mastercard's testing glossary spells the Agent Pay tag agent-pay-auth in lower case.
Mastercard's guide says Visa uses the tags agent-browser-auth and agent-payer-auth and generic agents such as ChatGPT use web-bot-auth.
The Level 1 guide's example request uses the header Signature-Agent with the value https://agentpay-key-directory.mastercard.com/.
The host agentpay-key-directory.mastercard.com did not resolve in DNS on 2026-10-11.
Cloudflare says Visa and Mastercard host their own directories of registered agent public keys and names no Mastercard directory URL.
Cloudflare says Agent Pay uses Web Bot Auth as its agent authentication layer.
Cloudflare's verification checks are header presence, key fetch by keyid, created and expires window, nonce uniqueness, tag validity, signature base reconstruction and Ed25519 verification.
Agent request signatures follow RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, published in February 2024.
Mastercard's Agent User Identity object carries mastercardIdToken, signature, kid, nonce and alg.
Mastercard says the mastercardIdToken is a JWT compatible with OpenID Connect ID Tokens and aligned with EMVCo Secure Remote Commerce.
Mastercard's Payment Data object carries paymentData, signature, kid, nonce and alg, signed with the same key and nonce as the HTTP message signature.
For form-fill checkouts the Payment Data object holds a hash of the tokenized payment data, which the merchant can compare with what its form received.
Mastercard's Intent API registers an agent-captured intent and returns an intentId with tokenized payment credentials.
Mastercard names intent fields intentId, intentSummary, intentStatus, orders, consumer and digitalAccountCredentials.
Mastercard's order object includes orderExecutionType with values IMMEDIATE and DEFERRED and an orderExpiry in UTC epoch seconds.
Mastercard identifies merchants in intents with srcDpaId, a Mastercard-generated identifier.
Mastercard tells merchants to reject a checkout whose total exceeds orderTotalAmount or whose srcDpaId differs from the intent.
Mastercard says the Level 3 Agent Pay payment payload contains a DSRP cryptogram and card metadata.
Mastercard labels the exchange of intent data between agent and merchant as future facing and part of Level 3.
Mastercard directs Agent Pay integrators to Mastercard Virtual Card Tokens for web guest checkouts with a simple form.
A one-time DTVC may be requested after user validation and consent to fill the security code field of a checkout form.
Mastercard validates the DTVC at authorization and tells the issuer whether DTVC validation was performed.
Mastercard's pages expand DTVC both as Dynamic Token Validation Code and as Dynamic Token Verification Code.
A DTVC is a one-time security code issued with a virtual card token, not an agentic token itself.
Mastercard says regional live agentic transactions were authenticated with Mastercard Payment Passkeys.
The Mastercard Developers llms.txt index listed no Agent Pay service on 2026-10-11.
Mastercard Developers lists an Agent Suite for Merchants product described as bringing agentic commerce to merchants through a single integration.
No public Agent Pay SDK, API reference or sandbox was found as of 2026-10-11.
The Mastercard Developers Agent Toolkit is an MCP server and library that exposes Mastercard documentation and API specifications to AI assistants.
The Agent Toolkit's API client reads only llms.txt and llms-full.txt documentation files from developer.mastercard.com and makes no payment calls.
The npm package @mastercard/developers-mcp was at version 0.1.7 on 2026-10-11.
The npm package @mastercard/developers-agent-toolkit was at version 0.1.6 on 2026-10-11.
The mastercard/developers-agent-toolkit repository is MIT licensed and was created on 2025-07-22.
The Verifiable Intent CHANGELOG dates version 0.1.0 to 2026-02-19.
The Verifiable Intent specification documents carry version 0.1-draft and the date 2026-02-18.
The git tag v0.1.0 points to the repository's initial commit dated 2026-03-05, and no GitHub release object exists.
Verifiable Intent pull request 23, merged on 2026-04-20, renamed constraint prefixes from payment.* to mandate.payment.* and moved cnf.kid to cnf.jwk.kid.
The 2026-04 Verifiable Intent changes added risk_data, versioned VCT suffixes, a per-constraint policy and the match_mode field without a new version number.
At tag v0.1.0 the Verifiable Intent mandate types were mandate.checkout, mandate.payment, mandate.checkout.open and mandate.payment.open, without a .1 suffix.
At tag v0.1.0 the amount constraint was named payment.amount; on main it is mandate.payment.amount_range.
The Verifiable Intent CHANGELOG says five constraint types while spec/constraints.md registers eight.
No commits were made to the Verifiable Intent main branch after 2026-04-20 as of 2026-10-11.
The Verifiable Intent repository had 97 stars and 20 forks on 2026-10-11.
The Verifiable Intent reference SDK is not published on PyPI.
The npm package named verifiable-intent is an unofficial TypeScript port by an individual developer, not a release of the agent-intent organization.
Verifiable Intent defines a layered SD-JWT credential chain from credential provider to user to agent.
Verifiable Intent has two execution modes: Immediate with two layers and Autonomous with three layers.
Verifiable Intent L1 is an SD-JWT with typ sd+jwt, signed by the Issuer, with a recommended lifetime of about one year.
Verifiable Intent L2 Immediate uses typ kb-sd-jwt and has a recommended lifetime of about 15 minutes (SHOULD be no more than 15 minutes from iat).
Verifiable Intent L2 Autonomous uses typ kb-sd-jwt+kb with a recommended lifetime of 24 hours to 30 days (SHOULD be no more than 30 days from iat) that must not exceed the L1 expiry.
Verifiable Intent L3a and L3b use typ kb-sd-jwt with a recommended lifetime of 5 minutes and a maximum of one hour.
L3a carries the final payment mandate to the payment network and L3b carries the final checkout mandate to the merchant.
Each Verifiable Intent layer binds the next through the RFC 7800 cnf claim.
In Autonomous mode both L2 mandates must carry an identical cnf.jwk with a kid that binds the agent's key.
Immediate mode L2 mandates must not contain a cnf claim, which signals that no further delegation is allowed.
L3 headers must carry a kid matching the L2 cnf.jwk.kid and must not carry a jwk parameter.
L3 payloads must not contain a cnf claim, making L3 the terminal delegation.
The L1 payload requires iss, sub, iat, exp, vct, cnf, _sd_alg and _sd, with email as a selectively disclosable claim.
Under the Mastercard reference profile the L1 vct must be https://credentials.mastercard.com/card and pan_last_four and scheme are required always-visible claims.
The L2 payload requires nonce, aud, iat, exp, sd_hash, delegate_payload, _sd_alg and _sd, with optional iss.
In L2 the aud claim identifies the agent; in L3a it identifies the payment network and in L3b the merchant.
The four Verifiable Intent mandate types on main are mandate.checkout.open.1, mandate.checkout.1, mandate.payment.open.1 and mandate.payment.1.
A final payment mandate contains vct, payment_instrument, payment_amount, payee and transaction_id.
A final checkout mandate contains vct, checkout_jwt and checkout_hash, and in L3b may add line_items and prompt_summary.
payment_amount holds a currency code and an integer amount in ISO 4217 minor units.
The payment_instrument object has type, id and an optional description, with mastercard.srcDigitalCard as the example type.
The open payment mandate may carry risk_data with device_id and ip_address, which is never copied into L3.
checkout_hash is the base64url SHA-256 of the checkout_jwt string, and the payment mandate carries the same value as transaction_id.
In Autonomous mode L3a transaction_id must equal L3b checkout_hash.
The mandate.payment.reference constraint carries conditional_transaction_id, a hash of the L2 checkout mandate disclosure, and is mandatory in Autonomous payment mandates.

Verifiable Intent registers eight constraint types: mandate.checkout.allowed_merchants, mandate.checkout.line_items, mandate.payment.allowed_payees, mandate.payment.amount_range, mandate.payment.budget, mandate.payment.recurrence, mandate.payment.agent_recurrence and mandate.payment.reference.
mandate.payment.amount_range has a currency and optional min and max in integer minor units and applies per transaction.
mandate.payment.budget sets a cumulative maximum that the payment network must track across transactions.
mandate.payment.agent_recurrence requires a start_date and end_date and must be accompanied by amount_range and budget constraints.
mandate.payment.recurrence authorizes a merchant-managed subscription setup, and later recurring charges happen outside the Verifiable Intent chain.
Verifiable Intent recurrence frequencies use ISO 20022 codes such as MNTH, and agent_recurrence also accepts ON_DEMAND.
mandate.checkout.line_items accepts an optional match_mode of minimum, the default, or exact.
Verifiable Intent constraint validation has a PERMISSIVE default mode that skips unknown types and a STRICT mode that rejects them.
Verifiable Intent says verifiers must reject open mandates that contain unknown constraint types regardless of strictness mode.
Verifiable Intent requires ES256 signatures and sha-256 as the selective disclosure hash algorithm.
Verifiable Intent builds on SD-JWT as defined in RFC 9901, published in November 2025.
Verifiable Intent says payment networks validate the credential chain as a pre-authorization step while the issuer makes the final authorization decision.
Verifiable Intent requires payment networks to enforce one L3a and L3b pair per L2 mandate pair and to track cumulative L3 spend per L2.
The Verifiable Intent Issuer can be a bank or a payment network such as Mastercard acting on the bank's behalf and must publish a JWKS endpoint.
Verifiable Intent recommends a clock skew tolerance of 300 seconds.
Verifiable Intent lists transport protocols, key provisioning, credential provider enrollment, dispute resolution and regulatory compliance mapping as out of scope.
Verifiable Intent v0.1 defines no credential revocation protocol and relies on short lifetimes and JWKS key removal.
The Verifiable Intent security model names RFC 9701 Token Status Lists as a possible future revocation mechanism.
Verifiable Intent says the always-visible sub claim lets verifiers link a user's transactions for the life of the L1 credential.
Verifiable Intent says its reference implementation uses fixed deterministic keys suitable only for testing.

The Verifiable Intent threat model covers replay, cross-merchant replay, constraint stripping, checkout-payment mismatch, algorithm confusion, clock skew, disclosure withholding, type confusion and split-agent attacks.
Verifiable Intent says budget and transaction count enforcement cannot be done cryptographically and requires stateful tracking by the payment network.
Verifiable Intent says it provides evidence for disputes but does not assign liability, specify chargeback codes or define arbitration.
The Verifiable Intent design rationale says its constraints give a cryptographic form of PSD2 dynamic linking but that it does not replace SCA.
The Verifiable Intent README says its regulatory references are informational and make no compliance claims.
The checkout_jwt schema, signing algorithm and verification are implementation-defined in Verifiable Intent v0.1.
An open issue reports that Verifiable Intent L2 lists each mandate digest in both _sd and delegate_payload, which RFC 9901 says verifiers must reject.
RFC 9901 states that the same digest value must not appear more than once in an SD-JWT.
An unattributed inline answer in Verifiable Intent issue 15 says liability shift work for the Agent Pay Acceptance Framework is ongoing.
The Verifiable Intent site says it ships integration mappings for AP2, ACP and UCP.
Verifiable Intent defines an optional agent_attestation claim with type and value but no attestation scheme yet.
On main, Verifiable Intent uses the same four mandate vct values as AP2 v0.2.
AP2 schemas name the amount constraint payment.amount_range while Verifiable Intent names it mandate.payment.amount_range: aligned semantics, different key prefixes.
The Verifiable Intent commit of 2026-04-18 is titled field alignment per AP2 schema updates.
Verifiable Intent's protocol page says AP2 leaves the verifiable digital credential format open and that VI provides a concrete option.
No public source documents live use of Verifiable Intent inside an AP2 flow.
Cloudflare says Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay both build on Web Bot Auth, use a tag in Signature-Input and require a nonce.
Visa TAP and Agent Pay use separate key directories hosted by each network.
In the ACP JSON schema of 2026-04-17, mastercard appears only as a card brand and 3DS directory server value.
An ACP payment processed through Stripe can carry a Mastercard agentic network token inside a Shared Payment Token.
Mastercard's developer guide says OpenAI discontinued ChatGPT Instant Checkout in March 2026.
Mastercard is listed as an endorser of the Universal Commerce Protocol.
Verifiable Intent says its credentials can be carried in UCP's AP2 mandate extension, which it names dev.ucp.shopping.ap2_mandate.
UCP renamed its AP2 extension to dev.ucp.common.payment.ap2_mandate (schema at main); the release v2026-08-25 notes spell the migrated extension ap2_mandates.
No documented integration between Agent Pay and UCP was found.
Mastercard's own AP4M text does not claim Machine Payments Protocol compatibility.
In Mastercard's AP4M release Tempo says it is working with Mastercard on Machine Payments Protocol compatibility, with Tempo providing stablecoin settlement.
No Mastercard-maintained MPP payment method exists in the MPP repositories; the MPP card method draft is authored by Visa.
Mastercard is a premier member of the x402 Foundation.
Coinbase's quote in the AP4M release names x402 as an open standard it brings to the work with Mastercard.
No documented relation links Agent Pay to ERC-8004.
EMVCo published a draft EMV Agentic Payments Framework for Specifications on 2026-09-01 with comments due 2026-09-30.
EMVCo says its proposed Intent Services would complement cryptographic solutions such as Verifiable Intent.
EMVCo says it may consider Know Your Agent and Agentic Transaction Indicators in future publications.
Mastercard does not publish a self-service price table for Agent Pay.
No agent-specific interchange, tokenization fee, liability rule or chargeback reason code for Agent Pay was published as of 2026-10-11.
A May 2026 note found no new agentic interchange categories disclosed by card networks and expected new fee categories in future.
Mastercard says standard chargeback rights and dispute processes apply to agentic transactions.
Mastercard has published no Agent Pay transaction volume or value figures.
Most Agent Pay transactions named in Mastercard releases were run in controlled environments or pilots.
Mastercard projects that one in 10 consumers will routinely use agents to make purchases by 2030.
Agent Pay's Level 1 and DTVC paths still require agents to fill human checkout forms on merchant websites.
A probability score for AI-initiated transactions implies that agent involvement is not always marked reliably in authorization traffic.
The Level 1 guide's sample verification code accepts only the two Visa tag values, not the Mastercard tag.
The 2026-03-05 Verifiable Intent announcement and the Mastercard Agent Pay product page could not be read directly because mastercard.com returns HTTP 403 to automated clients.

Mastercard's Level 1 to 3 agentic commerce guides and Checkout Solutions release history are the primary developer records found for Agent Pay; the use-case page use-cases/agent-pay/index.md returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-13 and the HTML page is a JavaScript shell, so its current content could not be read.
No academic paper analyzing Agent Pay or Verifiable Intent was found; arXiv 2609.27452 on issuer-sovereign agentic payments is the closest.
The arXiv paper A Formal Analysis of Agent Payment Protocols, posted 2026-08-30, models x402, MPP, ACP and AP2 but not Agent Pay.
No CVE or published attack specific to Agent Pay was found as of 2026-10-11.
Mastercard's Level 1 guide says networks and EMVCo are still developing 3DS support and decoupled authentication for agentic flows.
Mastercard's guide suggests that for deferred orders the merchant require the agent to obtain explicit consumer confirmation when intent validation fails.
For Level 3 direct payments the Payment Data object holds a hash of the credentials submitted.
Mastercard names order fields orderId, orderExecutionType, orderStatus, orderExpiry, orderTotalAmount, items, merchants and orderDeliveryDetails.
Mastercard names item fields itemId, itemName, itemDescription, itemUnitPrice, itemQuantity, itemDeliveryMethod, itemUrl, itemImageUrl and itemMetadata.
Mastercard names intent merchant fields srcDpaId, merchantName, merchantUrl and merchantLogoUrl.
The Level 1 guide example signature covers the components @authority and @path.
The Level 1 guide gives ed25519 and ecdsa-p256-sha256 as example alg values for agent request signatures.
The Level 2 guide gives PS256 and ES256 as example alg values for the Agent User Identity and Payment Data signatures.
Verifiable Intent issue 29, opened on 2026-07-17, says the @sd-jwt/core 0.20.0 library rejects every VI L2 credential, and had no maintainer response as of 2026-10-11.
The Verifiable Intent specification examples in section 11 list each L2 mandate digest in both _sd and delegate_payload.
The Verifiable Intent payee object has an optional id and required name and website.
The Verifiable Intent README gives its status as Draft (v0.1).
The Verifiable Intent Python package is version 0.1.0 and requires Python 3.10 or later and cryptography 42.0 or later.
The AP4M release targets machine payments that may be only fractions of a cent.
The Verifiable Intent L1 header requires alg ES256, typ sd+jwt and the kid of the issuer key.
The Verifiable Intent L2 header requires alg ES256 and a typ of kb-sd-jwt or kb-sd-jwt+kb, with an optional kid.
The Mastercard Developers MCP server runs locally with npx -y @mastercard/developers-mcp.
Verifiable Intent lists delegate_payload references so that a verifier can see that mandates exist even when their content is withheld.
Verifiable Intent says a split-agent attack is prevented by requiring an identical cnf.jwk in both mandates of an Autonomous pair.
Mastercard says merchants can verify agent signatures in their own backend or let a CDN do it.
Verifiable Intent proposes ACP extensions as a carrier for its credentials but defines no ACP binding.

Mastercard's Level 1 decision table sends requests without Signature-Input and a scheme tag to the non-agent bot policy and blocks requests with a missing required field or a key not found in the directory.
